name: Dana Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a senior researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. Tell me about a usual shift.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 43 and have handled contact-centre calls and chats for years. I finished secondary school and work at about the usual experienced-agent pace. I earn above the usual rate because I cover the Saturday queue. I use AI every day to sort old messages and flag repeat delivery questions, but I check the order before I answer.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part of that day stays with you after work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner, Bruno, and I have two children in school and a mortgage. Bruno repairs household appliances, and we have around nine months of expenses saved. Plenty of other centres are nearby. I like a busy Saturday when people finally get their parcels sorted. What wears me out is seeing a smooth wrong answer copied into three chats.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AI Plateau looks like my message sorter: useful for finding an old delivery promise, but not the final word. I would keep the order page beside the draft.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the Saturday queue stays, and nine months saved makes the mortgage feel manageable. Bruno’s repair income can vary, so I still like having money set aside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep answering Saturday calls and checking the sorter’s suggested dates. In the first year of small change, I’d put part of each Saturday premium into the house reserve and show a new agent how to find the original promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the work, attentive to mistakes. A copied delivery error can grow legs before anyone checks the first order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What copied error have you caught?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I once saw a draft repeat an old address after a customer had moved the delivery. I opened the new order, found the right building and called her back before the driver left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why keep saving with nine months?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bruno (my partner) and I keep the reserve for the mortgage and a slow repair month. I would not spend it just because the new sorter saves five minutes.

I’d keep the **order page** beside each draft.
think: I think the **Saturday queue** remains here.
I still protect savings against **variable repair income**.
I still want the **reserve ready** for a slow repair month.
do: Keep **Saturday calls** and verify suggested dates in 2026.
Save part of the **Saturday premium** during the first year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues Steady Disruption will move standard delivery answers to software, and we should show the company the wrong ones before it changes Saturday staffing. I would ask for a paid trial of the new system with a real error log.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think some of my Saturday calls may vanish; knowing the current tools does not make my paid hours safe. Nine months saved buys time to compare roles, but Bruno’s repair wage alone does not cover the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d take a paid trial of the new answer system if it lets agents record mistakes and test twenty changed deliveries. In the first year routine replies move, I’d apply for a posted paid quality-check role only if the offered wage and weekly hours cover the mortgage and replace enough Saturday premium.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but curious about the trial. I do not want to call an error log a job until someone puts hours beside it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the trial count?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would count wrong addresses and whether the customer called again. Another agent could check the same cases before I show the figures at a team meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you judge the offer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare a full week’s pay, not just a tempting hourly rate. Saturday money is part of our house budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2028 could read, answer and check a whole delivery case. I would ask for posted paid quality openings and a date for the Saturday rota change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think cheap thinking AI could take most of my Saturday headset work in 2028. Robots arrive around 2031 and do not give my screen work three more years; nine months saved is a search window, not a salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d postpone a planned home office desk and hold the money with our mortgage reserve. In the first year after 2028, I’d apply for a posted paid quality role only if its offered wage and hours cover our mortgage, and take a paid trial to see the real error queue before accepting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, though I have time for a careful search. Nine months in the bank cannot make a vanished Saturday shift come back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say about the desk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Bruno (my partner) we can keep the old desk another year. It wobbles but can be fixed; we need cash more than new furniture if my shift ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the quality manager?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the quality manager how many people actually work on corrections and what they are paid. If there is no posted opening, I would keep looking at the other centres rather than volunteer for free.

I’d say **2028 thinking AI** reaches headset work first.

I see **nine months saved** as search time, not a salary.

fieldNote: She anchors risk to **2028 thinking AI**.

steps.text: Keep the usable old home office desk instead of buying another

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives us time to test whether human corrections remain a paid job. I would ask the centre to show posted hours rather than call every agent a future supervisor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years could get me into quality checks if real openings survive. Full AGI might do those checks too, so I would not borrow for a certificate that has no posted destination.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From 2026 I’d take a funded service-quality course on paid time only if a posted paid opening requires it, and ask for one paid shift in the correction queue if offered. In the first year after 2031, I’d apply for that quality role only if a written wage and weekly hours cover our mortgage; otherwise I’d keep paid calls while looking nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I can test a real queue before a move. A paid correction shift tells me more than a promise that every agent will supervise software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a correction shift reveal?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for three wrong delivery decisions and see who has the authority to change each one. If the worker can only send a form, the role is not the job I was promised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Bruno need in writing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show Bruno (my partner) the posted pay and the course hours before I enroll. Our mortgage reserve is for the house, not a hopeful badge.

I’d demand proof that **human quality roles** remain paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2036 gives us a decade to compare actual paid jobs and keep a place for people learning the first shift. I would show new agents the old delivery promise before teaching a shortcut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could keep the Saturday wage for years and build more savings. Full thinking AI could still take calls by 2036, while robots around 2039 are later for hands-on work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep Saturday calls, save a set part of the premium and ask for a yearly list of paid quality vacancies. In the first year after 2036, I’d apply for a posted paid correction role only if my call hours fall and a written offer covers the mortgage with steady weekly hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the far date, calm enough about next month. A decade before AGI in 2036 lets me test work while keeping the mortgage paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach a new agent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show a new agent how to read the updated address before sending a reply. My first trainer let me correct a mistake while she stayed on the call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move the family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the children in their school unless Bruno (my partner) and I had a signed offer and a manageable journey. Plenty of centres nearby mean we can look without moving first.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, even though I use AI every day. A cheaper system that reads and answers the whole delivery case could end my Saturday wage. I would need a written staffing date, a posted paid quality role with mortgage-covering hours, and a paid trial before treating it as secure.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether the customer ever sees the error log. A customer should be able to see which delivery promise was wrong and who can correct it.

headlineQuote: A customer should be able to see which delivery promise was wrong and who can correct it.
portrait: At **43**, Dana is an experienced average-skill agent after secondary school with higher Saturday pay.
She and Bruno support **two schoolchildren** and a mortgage with nine months saved.
She uses **AI daily** to sort messages while checking the underlying order.
She seeks **paid quality work** and clear error records as routine replies move.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove her Saturday delivery work despite daily AI skill.
whatWouldHelp: A **written staffing date**, posted paid quality role and paid trial would help.
